title: Language: Basic concepts, theories and pedagogy. English in Use.
overview: Is unit mein linguistics ke basic concepts (Saussure, Chomsky, Halliday, speech acts, Grice), phonetics se semantics tak, sociolinguistics, history of English, ELT methods aur testing, aur grammar-usage aate hain. NET mein yahan se zyadatar 'kisne kaha/kis book mein', match-the-following, chronology aur sahi-galat sentence wale direct sawal aate hain.

topics.title: Ferdinand de Saussure and Structuralism
points: Saussure (1857-1913), Swiss linguist, is called the father of modern linguistics and of structuralism.
Course in General Linguistics (Cours de linguistique generale, 1916) was published posthumously, compiled from students' lecture notes by Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye.
Langue = the abstract, shared system of a language; Parole = the individual, concrete act of speaking (langue = niyam-vyavastha, parole = asli bolna). Langage = the general human faculty of language.
The linguistic sign has two sides: signifier (sound-image) and signified (concept); their relation is arbitrary.
Language is a system of differences: 'In language there are only differences without positive terms.'
Synchronic study = language at one point in time; diachronic study = language change over time. Saussure gave priority to synchronic study.
Syntagmatic relations = linear, chain relations (horizontal); paradigmatic relations (Saussure called them associative) = relations of substitution (vertical).
Saussure's comparison: language is like a game of chess - value of a piece depends on its position in the system.
He proposed 'semiology' (semiologie), a science of signs; C. S. Peirce independently developed 'semiotics' (icon, index, symbol).

American structuralism: Edward Sapir, Language (1921); Leonard Bloomfield, Language (1933), behaviourist, immediate constituent analysis; Prague School (Trubetzkoy, Jakobson) developed functional phonology.

topics.title: Noam Chomsky and Generative Grammar
points: Syntactic Structures (1957) launched Transformational Generative Grammar (TGG) - the 'Chomskyan revolution'.
Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965) gave the 'Standard Theory': competence vs performance, deep structure vs surface structure.
Competence = speaker's unconscious knowledge of the language; Performance = actual use in concrete situations (compare Saussure's langue/parole).
Example sentence 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' shows a sentence can be grammatical yet meaningless (Syntactic Structures, 1957).
'A Review of B. F. Skinner's Verbal Behavior' (1959, in Language) attacked behaviourist accounts of language learning.
Innateness hypothesis: children have a Language Acquisition Device (LAD) and Universal Grammar (UG); 'poverty of the stimulus' argument.
Later models: Extended Standard Theory (1970s), Government and Binding Theory - Lectures on Government and Binding (1981), Principles and Parameters, The Minimalist Program (1995).
Other works: Cartesian Linguistics (1966), Language and Mind (1968), The Sound Pattern of English (1968, with Morris Halle).
Chomsky's grammar is formal and mentalist; it is criticised by Dell Hymes, who proposed 'communicative competence' (1972).
Three levels of adequacy: observational, descriptive and explanatory adequacy.

topics.title: M. A. K. Halliday and Functional Linguistics
points: Halliday (1925-2018), pupil of J. R. Firth, founded Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL); language is a 'social semiotic'.
Works: Learning How to Mean (1975), Language as Social Semiotic (1978), An Introduction to Functional Grammar (1985), Cohesion in English (1976, with Ruqaiya Hasan).
Three metafunctions: ideational (experiential + logical), interpersonal, textual.
Register variables: Field (what is happening), Tenor (who is taking part), Mode (role of language, spoken/written).
Seven functions of child language (Halliday): instrumental, regulatory, interactional, personal, heuristic, imaginative, representational/informative.
Cohesion in English names five cohesive devices: reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, lexical cohesion.
Theme-Rheme: Theme is the starting point of a clause; Rheme is the rest (Prague School, Mathesius, developed by Halliday).
J. R. Firth (London School) - 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps' (1957); context of situation (from Malinowski).
Bronislaw Malinowski coined 'phatic communion' (1923) - talk for social contact, e.g. 'Nice weather!'.
Roman Jakobson's six functions of language ('Linguistics and Poetics', 1960): emotive, conative, referential, poetic, phatic, metalingual.

topics.title: Speech Act Theory: Austin and Searle
points: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (1962), from William James Lectures at Harvard (1955).
Austin first distinguished constatives (true/false statements) and performatives (utterances that do an act, e.g. 'I name this ship...').
Three acts: locutionary (saying with meaning), illocutionary (force - promising, warning), perlocutionary (effect on hearer - persuading, frightening).
Felicity conditions: conditions that must be met for a performative to succeed; failures are 'infelicities' (misfires and abuses).
Austin's five classes of illocutionary verbs: verdictives, exercitives, commissives, behabitives, expositives.
John R. Searle, Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language (1969); 'Indirect Speech Acts' (1975); Expression and Meaning (1979).
Searle's taxonomy: representatives (assertives), directives, commissives, expressives, declarations.
Indirect speech act: 'Can you pass the salt?' - question form, request function.
Searle's felicity conditions: propositional content, preparatory, sincerity and essential conditions.
Derrida criticised Austin in 'Signature Event Context' (1972), leading to the Derrida-Searle debate.

topics.title: Grice, Politeness and Pragmatics
points: Charles Morris (Foundations of the Theory of Signs, 1938) divided semiotics into syntax, semantics and pragmatics.
H. P. Grice, 'Logic and Conversation' (1975; William James Lectures, Harvard, 1967); earlier essay 'Meaning' (1957).
Cooperative Principle: 'Make your conversational contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs...'
Four maxims: Quantity (be as informative as required), Quality (be truthful), Relation (be relevant), Manner (be clear, brief, orderly).
Flouting a maxim openly creates conversational implicature; violating secretly misleads (jhooth bolna = violation).
Conventional implicature is tied to words like 'but', 'even'; conversational implicature depends on context.
Geoffrey Leech, Principles of Pragmatics (1983): Politeness Principle with maxims of tact, generosity, approbation, modesty, agreement, sympathy.
Brown and Levinson, Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage (1978/1987): positive face, negative face, face-threatening acts (FTAs); 'face' from Erving Goffman.
Deixis: person (I, you), place (here, there), time (now, then), social and discourse deixis.
Relevance Theory: Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson, Relevance: Communication and Cognition (1986).

topics.title: Phonetics
points: Branches: articulatory (production), acoustic (physical sound waves), auditory (perception).
International Phonetic Association founded in Paris (1886); the IPA chart is used to transcribe sounds.
Received Pronunciation (RP) has 44 phonemes: 24 consonants and 20 vowels (12 pure vowels/monophthongs + 8 diphthongs).
RP has 7 short vowels and 5 long vowels; 8 diphthongs: /eɪ, aɪ, ɔɪ, aʊ, əʊ, ɪə, eə, ʊə/ (centring and closing).
Places of articulation: bilabial (p, b, m), labiodental (f, v), dental (th sounds), alveolar (t, d, s, z, n, l), post-alveolar, palatal (j), velar (k, g, ng), glottal (h).
Manners of articulation: plosive/stop, fricative, affricate (ch, j as in church, judge), nasal, lateral (l), approximant (r, w, j).
Voiced sounds vibrate the vocal cords (b, d, g, v, z); voiceless do not (p, t, k, f, s).
Schwa /ə/ is the most frequent vowel in English, found in weak/unstressed syllables (e.g. first vowel of 'about').

Daniel Jones devised the Cardinal Vowels and wrote English Pronouncing Dictionary (1917) and An Outline of English Phonetics (1918); A. C. Gimson wrote An Introduction to the Pronunciation of English (1962).
English is a stress-timed language (stress comes at regular intervals); French and most Indian languages are syllable-timed.
Syllable structure: onset + rhyme (nucleus + coda); nucleus is usually a vowel; English allows up to 3 consonants in onset (e.g. 'strengths' has a complex coda).

topics.title: Phonology
points: Phonology studies the sound system/patterns of a language; phonetics studies speech sounds physically.
Phoneme = smallest contrastive sound unit that changes meaning; written between slashes /p/.
Allophones = variants of one phoneme, in square brackets: aspirated [ph] in 'pin' vs unaspirated [p] in 'spin'.
Minimal pair = two words differing in one sound only: pin/bin, ship/sheep.
Complementary distribution = allophones never occur in the same environment; free variation = interchangeable without meaning change.
Connected speech processes: assimilation ('ten boys' -> tem boys), elision (dropping sounds, 'next day'), linking r and intrusive r, juncture.
Suprasegmental features: stress, pitch, intonation, rhythm, tone, length, juncture.
N. S. Trubetzkoy, Principles of Phonology (Grundzuge der Phonologie, 1939) - Prague School; Roman Jakobson developed distinctive features.
Chomsky and Halle, The Sound Pattern of English (1968) founded generative phonology.
Phonotactics = rules about permissible sound sequences (English words cannot begin with /ng/).

topics.title: Morphology and Word Formation
points: Morphology studies word structure; the term was introduced into linguistics in the 19th century (from Goethe's biological use).
Morpheme = smallest meaningful unit; free morphemes stand alone (book), bound morphemes cannot (-s, un-).
Derivational morphemes create new words/change class (happy -> happiness); inflectional morphemes mark grammar only.
English has 8 inflectional morphemes: plural -s, possessive -'s, 3rd person singular -s, past -ed, past participle -en, progressive -ing, comparative -er, superlative -est.
Allomorphs = variants of a morpheme: plural /s/ (cats), /z/ (dogs), /iz/ (buses); zero morpheme in 'sheep'.
Blending: smog (smoke + fog), brunch, motel; Lewis Carroll called such words 'portmanteau' words in Through the Looking-Glass (1871).
Clipping: ad (advertisement), flu (influenza), exam; Back-formation: edit (from editor), televise (from television), babysit.
Acronym is read as a word (NATO, laser, scuba); initialism is read letter by letter (BBC, FBI).
Conversion (zero derivation/functional shift): noun to verb, e.g. 'to google', 'to bottle'.
Coinage/eponym: Kleenex, xerox, sandwich (from Earl of Sandwich), boycott; compounding: blackboard, greenhouse.

topics.title: Syntax
points: Syntax studies how words combine into phrases, clauses and sentences.
Immediate Constituent (IC) analysis: Bloomfield (1933) and Rulon Wells ('Immediate Constituents', 1947).
Phrase Structure (PS) rules: S -> NP + VP; NP -> Det + N; VP -> V + NP (Chomsky, 1957).
X-bar theory: Chomsky ('Remarks on Nominalization', 1970), developed by Ray Jackendoff (1977).
Structural ambiguity: 'Flying planes can be dangerous'; 'Old men and women'; 'Visiting relatives can be boring'.
Quirk et al., A Comprehensive Grammar of the English Language (1985): clause elements S, V, O, C, A and seven basic clause patterns (SV, SVO, SVC, SVA, SVOO, SVOC, SVOA).
Sentence types by structure: simple, compound (coordination), complex (subordination), compound-complex.
Sentence types by function: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory.
English basic word order is SVO; Hindi is SOV.
Recursion = a rule can apply repeatedly, producing infinitely long sentences ('the house that Jack built').

topics.title: Semantics
points: Michel Breal coined 'semantique' (1883); Essai de semantique (1897).
C. K. Ogden and I. A. Richards, The Meaning of Meaning (1923): semiotic/semantic triangle - symbol, thought/reference, referent.
Geoffrey Leech, Semantics (1974): seven types of meaning - conceptual, connotative, social, affective, reflected, collocative, thematic.
Sense vs reference: Gottlob Frege, 'On Sense and Reference' (Uber Sinn und Bedeutung, 1892); 'morning star' and 'evening star' have one referent.
Lexical relations: synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy (rose is hyponym of flower; flower is hypernym/superordinate), meronymy (part-whole), homonymy, polysemy.
Antonym types: gradable (hot/cold), complementary/binary (alive/dead), converse/relational (buy/sell, husband/wife).
Homonyms: same form, unrelated meanings (bank of river / bank for money); polysemy: one word, related meanings (head of body / head of department).
Homophones sound alike (meet/meat); homographs are spelt alike (lead metal / lead verb).
Entailment: 'He killed the bug' entails 'The bug died'; presupposition survives negation ('His wife is ill' presupposes he has a wife).
Componential analysis: man = [+HUMAN, +ADULT, +MALE]; Prototype theory: Eleanor Rosch (1970s) - robin is a better example of 'bird' than penguin.

topics.title: Sociolinguistics
points: Sociolinguistics studies language in relation to society: class, region, gender, ethnicity, context.
Dialect = regional/social variety; idiolect = an individual's own speech; sociolect = class variety; register = variety according to use/situation.
Diglossia: Charles Ferguson, 'Diglossia' (1959) - High (H) and Low (L) varieties in one community (e.g. Arabic, Swiss German); extended by Joshua Fishman (1967).
Pidgin = contact language with no native speakers; creole = pidgin that becomes a mother tongue of a community (creolisation).
Code-switching = moving between languages across sentences; code-mixing = mixing within a sentence (Hinglish).
William Labov, The Social Stratification of English in New York City (1966) - department store study of post-vocalic /r/ (Saks, Macy's, S. Klein).
Basil Bernstein: restricted code and elaborated code (Class, Codes and Control, 1971).
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity): language shapes thought; strong version = linguistic determinism.
Braj B. Kachru's Three Concentric Circles of English (1985): Inner (UK, USA), Outer (India, Nigeria), Expanding (China, Japan); The Alchemy of English (1986).
Peter Trudgill studied Norwich English (1974); Howard Giles proposed Communication Accommodation Theory (convergence/divergence); Robin Lakoff, Language and Woman's Place (1975).

topics.title: History of the English Language
points: English belongs to the West Germanic branch of the Indo-European family; Sir William Jones (1786, Calcutta) noted Sanskrit's kinship with Greek and Latin.
Periods: Old English (c. 450-1100/1150), Middle English (c. 1100/1150-1500), Early Modern English (1500-1700/1800), Modern English.
Angles, Saxons and Jutes invaded Britain c. 449 AD (Bede). OE dialects: Northumbrian, Mercian, West Saxon (literary standard under King Alfred), Kentish.
Scandinavian (Viking) influence gave 'they, them, their', sky, skin, egg, law; Danelaw. Norman Conquest (1066) brought huge French influence.
English replaced French in law courts by the Statute of Pleading (1362); Chancery Standard shaped written English in the 15th century.
William Caxton set up the first printing press in England at Westminster (1476).
Great Vowel Shift (c. 1400-1700): long vowels were raised; term coined by Otto Jespersen.
Grimm's Law (Jacob Grimm, 1822; first noted by Rasmus Rask, 1818) - First Germanic Consonant Shift: p>f, t>th, k>h (pater/father); Verner's Law (1875) explained exceptions.
Milestones: King James (Authorised) Version of the Bible (1611); Samuel Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language (1755); OED first published as A New English Dictionary (1884-1928).
Key books: Otto Jespersen, Growth and Structure of the English Language (1905); A. C. Baugh, A History of the English Language (1935, later with Thomas Cable).
Renaissance 'inkhorn terms' controversy: over-use of Latinate words; Sir Thomas Elyot and others defended borrowing.

topics.title: ELT Methods: GTM, Direct Method, ALM and Humanistic Methods
points: Grammar Translation Method (GTM, also 'Prussian Method'): rules + translation, mother tongue used, reading/writing focus; associated with Karl Plotz, Seidenstucker, Ollendorf.
Reform Movement (1880s): Henry Sweet, Wilhelm Vietor ('Language teaching must start afresh', 1882), Paul Passy - priority of speech and phonetics.
Direct Method (Natural Method): no translation, target language only, inductive grammar; Maximilian Berlitz (Berlitz schools, 1878), Francois Gouin (Series Method), L. Sauveur.
Oral Approach / Situational Language Teaching (1930s-60s): Harold Palmer, A. S. Hornby; Michael West's New Method Readers and General Service List (1953).
Audio-Lingual Method (ALM, 'Army Method', WWII): based on structural linguistics and Skinner's behaviourism; habit formation, mim-mem, pattern drills; Charles Fries (Michigan).
Contrastive Analysis Hypothesis: Robert Lado, Linguistics Across Cultures (1957) - L1-L2 differences predict errors.
Silent Way: Caleb Gattegno (1963) - teacher silent, Cuisenaire rods, Fidel charts.
Community Language Learning (CLL): Charles A. Curran - counselling learning; teacher as 'knower', learner as 'client'.
Suggestopedia: Georgi Lozanov (Bulgaria, 1970s) - relaxation, baroque music, 'desuggestion'.
Total Physical Response (TPR): James Asher (1960s-77) - commands with body actions.
Bilingual Method: C. J. Dodson (1967); Structural Approach was popular in Indian schools (Madras 'Snowball' scheme).
Indian context: Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835); Kothari Commission (1964-66) and the Three-Language Formula (NPE 1968).

topics.title: CLT, TBLT, Krashen and SLA Theories
points: Communicative Language Teaching (CLT, 1970s): fluency over accuracy, meaning-focused; D. A. Wilkins, Notional Syllabuses (1976); H. G. Widdowson, Teaching Language as Communication (1978).

Dell Hymes coined 'communicative competence' ('On Communicative Competence', 1972); Canale and Swain (1980): grammatical, sociolinguistic, strategic competence; Canale (1983) added discourse competence.
Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT): N. S. Prabhu's Bangalore (Communicational Teaching) Project, 1979-84; Second Language Pedagogy (1987) - information-gap, reasoning-gap, opinion-gap tasks.
Jane Willis, A Framework for Task-Based Learning (1996): pre-task, task cycle (task, planning, report), language focus; David Nunan, Rod Ellis also central to TBLT.
Stephen Krashen's Monitor Model - five hypotheses: Acquisition-Learning, Monitor, Natural Order, Input (i+1), Affective Filter (Principles and Practice in Second Language Acquisition, 1982).
Natural Approach: Krashen and Tracy Terrell (1983).
Interlanguage: Larry Selinker (1972); fossilization = errors that become permanent.
Error Analysis: S. Pit Corder, 'The Significance of Learners' Errors' (1967) - errors (competence) vs mistakes (performance).
Interaction Hypothesis: Michael Long (1981/1996); Output Hypothesis: Merrill Swain (1985); Noticing Hypothesis: Richard Schmidt (1990).
Vygotsky: Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD); 'scaffolding' term by Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976).
Lexical Approach: Michael Lewis (1993); Postmethod condition/pedagogy: B. Kumaravadivelu (1994) - particularity, practicality, possibility.
PPP = Presentation, Practice, Production; ESA = Engage, Study, Activate (Jeremy Harmer).

topics.title: Language Testing and Evaluation
points: Validity = test measures what it claims to measure; types: content, construct, criterion-related (concurrent and predictive), face validity.
Reliability = consistency of results; measured by test-retest, parallel forms, split-half, inter-rater/intra-rater reliability.
Practicality (feasibility) and washback/backwash (effect of a test on teaching and learning - positive or negative).
Test types by purpose: proficiency (TOEFL, IELTS), achievement, diagnostic, placement, aptitude (MLAT by John Carroll and Stanley Sapon, 1959).
Formative evaluation = during the course for improvement; summative = at the end for grading; CCE = Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CBSE, 2009).
Norm-referenced tests compare a learner with others; criterion-referenced tests measure against fixed standards.
Discrete-point testing (Robert Lado, Language Testing, 1961) tests one item at a time; integrative tests (cloze, dictation) test many skills together.
Cloze procedure: Wilson L. Taylor (1953) - every nth word deleted; John Oller's Unitary Competence Hypothesis supported integrative testing.
Item analysis: facility value (difficulty index) and discrimination index.
Key texts: Arthur Hughes, Testing for Language Teachers (1989); Lyle Bachman, Fundamental Considerations in Language Testing (1990); Bloom's Taxonomy (1956).

topics.title: Grammar and Usage (English in Use)
points: Prescriptive grammar tells how one should speak (Robert Lowth, A Short Introduction to English Grammar, 1762; Lindley Murray, 1795); descriptive grammar records actual use.
Traditional grammar has eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.
'Neither...nor' / 'either...or': verb agrees with the nearer subject - 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present.'
'The number of students is...' (singular) but 'A number of students are...' (plural); 'Each/Every' takes a singular verb.
'One of the best books that have been written' - verb agrees with plural antecedent 'books'.
Correlatives: 'No sooner...than', 'Hardly/Scarcely...when', 'Lest...should' (never 'lest...not').
Inversion after negative adverbials: 'Never have I seen...'; 'Seldom does he come.'
Conditionals: zero (If you heat ice, it melts), first (If it rains, I will stay), second (If I were rich, I would...), third (If I had known, I would have...).
Dangling modifier: 'Walking down the road, the tree fell' (wrong); split infinitive: 'to boldly go'.
Reference works: H. W. Fowler, A Dictionary of Modern English Usage (1926); Quirk, Greenbaum, Leech, Svartvik, A Comprehensive Grammar of the English Language (1985).
Common errors: 'cousin brother' (Indian English), 'discuss about' (discuss takes no 'about'), 'return back', 'I am having a car' (stative verb in progressive).

terms.hindi: किसी भाषा की पूरी नियम-व्यवस्था जो सबके दिमाग में साझी होती है
terms.net: The abstract, social system of rules and conventions shared by a speech community; contrasted with parole by Saussure in Course in General Linguistics (1916).

terms.hindi: किसी व्यक्ति का असल में बोला या लिखा गया वाक्य
terms.net: The individual, concrete utterance or act of speech produced by a speaker using the system of langue (Saussure).

terms.hindi: शब्द की ध्वनि या लिखित रूप
terms.net: The sound-image or material form of a linguistic sign; paired with the signified (concept) by Saussure.

terms.hindi: शब्द सुनकर मन में आने वाला विचार
terms.net: The concept or mental idea to which a signifier refers; together they form the sign, whose relation Saussure called arbitrary.

terms.hindi: शब्द और उसके अर्थ के बीच कोई प्राकृतिक रिश्ता न होना
terms.net: The principle that there is no natural or necessary link between signifier and signified; a basic design feature of language (Saussure; Hockett).

terms.hindi: किसी एक समय पर भाषा का अध्ययन
terms.net: Study of a language as a system at a particular point in time, without reference to its history (Saussure).

terms.hindi: समय के साथ भाषा में आए बदलाव का अध्ययन
terms.net: Historical study of how a language changes over time; historical linguistics (Saussure).

terms.hindi: वाक्य में शब्दों का एक के बाद एक जुड़ना
terms.net: Linear relations between units that co-occur in a sequence or chain (horizontal axis of language).

terms.hindi: एक जगह पर बदले जा सकने वाले शब्दों का संबंध
terms.net: Relations of substitution between units that can replace each other in the same position (vertical axis); Saussure's 'associative' relations.

terms.hindi: भाषा के नियमों का अंदरूनी, अनजाना ज्ञान
terms.net: A native speaker's tacit, internalised knowledge of the grammar of the language; contrasted with performance by Chomsky in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965).

terms.hindi: असल स्थिति में भाषा का प्रयोग
terms.net: The actual use of language in concrete situations, affected by memory limits, distractions and errors (Chomsky).

terms.hindi: वाक्य का अंदरूनी, मूल अर्थ वाला ढाँचा
terms.net: The underlying abstract syntactic representation of a sentence from which surface structure is derived by transformations (Chomsky, 1965).

terms.hindi: बच्चे के दिमाग में भाषा सीखने की जन्मजात क्षमता
terms.net: A hypothesised innate mental faculty that enables children to acquire language rapidly from limited input (Chomsky).

terms.hindi: सभी भाषाओं में पाए जाने वाले साझा मूल नियम
terms.net: The set of innate principles and parameters common to all human languages, proposed by Chomsky.

terms.hindi: भाषा के तीन मुख्य काम - अनुभव, संबंध और पाठ बनाना
terms.net: In Halliday's Systemic Functional Linguistics, the three broad functions of language: ideational, interpersonal and textual.

terms.hindi: स्थिति के हिसाब से बदली हुई भाषा, जैसे क़ानूनी या डॉक्टरी भाषा
terms.net: A variety of language defined by its use in a particular situation, analysed by Halliday in terms of field, tenor and mode.

terms.hindi: पाठ के वाक्यों को आपस में जोड़ने वाले शब्दिक साधन
terms.net: The grammatical and lexical linking within a text (reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, lexical cohesion); Halliday and Hasan, Cohesion in English (1976).

terms.hindi: सिर्फ़ रिश्ता बनाए रखने के लिए की गई बातचीत, जैसे 'कैसे हो?'
terms.net: Language used to establish social contact rather than convey information; term coined by Bronislaw Malinowski (1923).

terms.hindi: ऐसा कथन जो बोलते ही कोई काम कर देता है, जैसे 'मैं वादा करता हूँ'
terms.net: An utterance that performs an action rather than describes a state of affairs, e.g. 'I promise'; contrasted with constative by J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (1962).

terms.hindi: कथन के पीछे का इरादा, जैसे चेतावनी देना या वादा करना
terms.net: The act performed in saying something, carrying a particular force such as promising, ordering or warning (Austin).

terms.hindi: कथन का सुनने वाले पर पड़ने वाला असर
terms.net: The consequential effect of an utterance on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening or convincing (Austin).

terms.hindi: किसी कथन के सफल होने के लिए ज़रूरी शर्तें
terms.net: The conditions that must be satisfied for a speech act to be successfully performed (Austin; refined by Searle).

terms.hindi: बातचीत में आपसी सहयोग का नियम
terms.net: Grice's principle that participants make their contribution such as is required by the accepted purpose of the talk; realised through the maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner ('Logic and Conversation', 1975).

terms.hindi: जो सीधे कहा नहीं गया पर इशारे से समझा गया अर्थ
terms.net: Meaning that is implied or suggested by an utterance beyond its literal content; term coined by H. P. Grice.

terms.hindi: ऐसे शब्द जिनका अर्थ संदर्भ पर निर्भर हो, जैसे 'यहाँ', 'मैं', 'अब'
terms.net: Words and expressions (I, here, now, this) whose reference depends on the context of utterance; types: person, place, time, social, discourse.

terms.hindi: कथन में पहले से मान ली गई बात
terms.net: An assumption taken for granted by an utterance, which remains true even when the sentence is negated.

terms.hindi: भाषा की सबसे छोटी ध्वनि इकाई जो अर्थ बदल दे
terms.net: The smallest contrastive unit in the sound system of a language that can distinguish meaning, e.g. /p/ and /b/ in pin/bin.

terms.hindi: एक ही ध्वनि के अलग-अलग उच्चारण रूप
terms.net: A predictable phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change meaning, e.g. aspirated [ph] in 'pin' vs [p] in 'spin'.

terms.hindi: ऐसे दो शब्द जिनमें सिर्फ़ एक ध्वनि का फ़र्क हो
terms.net: Two words that differ in only one sound segment and have different meanings, used to establish phonemes (ship/sheep).

terms.hindi: अंग्रेज़ी का सबसे कमज़ोर, बिना ज़ोर वाला 'अ' स्वर
terms.net: The mid-central unstressed vowel /ə/, the most frequent vowel in English, e.g. the first vowel of 'about'.

terms.hindi: एक अक्षर में दो स्वरों का मिला हुआ स्वर, जैसे 'आइ'
terms.net: A vowel sound involving a glide from one vowel quality to another within one syllable; RP has eight.

terms.hindi: पास वाली ध्वनि के असर से किसी ध्वनि का बदल जाना
terms.net: A connected-speech process in which a sound becomes more like a neighbouring sound, e.g. 'ten boys' pronounced 'tem boys'.

terms.hindi: शब्द-ध्वनियों से ऊपर के गुण जैसे ज़ोर, सुर और लय
terms.net: Phonological features extending over more than one segment: stress, pitch, intonation, rhythm and tone.

terms.hindi: शब्द का सबसे छोटा अर्थपूर्ण हिस्सा
terms.net: The smallest meaningful or grammatical unit of language; may be free (book) or bound (-s, un-).

terms.hindi: एक ही रूपिम के अलग-अलग रूप
terms.net: A variant form of a morpheme, e.g. the English plural realised as /s/, /z/ or /iz/.

terms.hindi: किसी लंबे शब्द से गलती से छोटा नया शब्द बना लेना
terms.net: Word formation by removing a supposed affix from an existing word, e.g. 'edit' from 'editor', 'televise' from 'television'.

terms.hindi: दो शब्दों के टुकड़े जोड़कर बना शब्द, जैसे smog
terms.net: A blend formed by combining parts of two words (smog, brunch); term used by Lewis Carroll's Humpty Dumpty in Through the Looking-Glass (1871).

terms.hindi: बिना बदलाव के शब्द की श्रेणी बदल देना, जैसे संज्ञा से क्रिया
terms.net: Change of a word's grammatical class without any affix, e.g. noun 'bottle' to verb 'to bottle'; also called zero derivation or functional shift.

terms.hindi: छोटे वर्ग का बड़े वर्ग में शामिल होना, जैसे गुलाब फूल का प्रकार है
terms.net: The sense relation of inclusion between a specific term (hyponym, rose) and a general term (hypernym/superordinate, flower).

terms.hindi: एक शब्द के कई जुड़े हुए अर्थ
terms.net: The existence of several related meanings for a single word, e.g. 'head' of body and 'head' of department; contrasted with homonymy.

terms.hindi: एक समाज में भाषा के दो रूप - एक औपचारिक, एक बोलचाल का
terms.net: A situation in which two varieties of a language, a High and a Low, are used for different social functions in one community; Charles Ferguson (1959).

terms.hindi: व्यापार आदि के लिए बनी मिली-जुली सरल भाषा, जिसका कोई मूल वक्ता न हो
terms.net: A simplified contact language that develops between groups with no common language and has no native speakers.

terms.hindi: ऐसी पिजिन भाषा जो किसी समुदाय की मातृभाषा बन गई हो
terms.net: A language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community, acquiring full grammatical complexity.

terms.hindi: बात करते समय एक भाषा से दूसरी भाषा में चले जाना
terms.net: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation by bilingual speakers.

terms.hindi: सीखने वाले की बीच की भाषा - न मातृभाषा, न पूरी लक्ष्य भाषा
terms.net: The learner's developing, systematic second-language system, intermediate between L1 and L2; term coined by Larry Selinker (1972).

terms.hindi: गलतियों का पक्का होकर स्थायी बन जाना
terms.net: The process by which incorrect L2 forms become permanent in a learner's interlanguage (Selinker).

terms.hindi: डर, चिंता जैसी भावनाएँ जो भाषा सीखने में रुकावट डालें
terms.net: Krashen's hypothesis that negative emotions such as anxiety and low motivation block comprehensible input from being acquired.

terms.hindi: ऐसी भाषा जो सीखने वाले के स्तर से थोड़ी ही ऊपर हो
terms.net: Krashen's Input Hypothesis: acquisition occurs when learners understand input slightly beyond their current level (i+1).

terms.hindi: परीक्षा का पढ़ाने और पढ़ने के तरीके पर पड़ने वाला असर
terms.net: The effect, positive or negative, of a test on teaching and learning; also called backwash.

terms.hindi: पाठ में से हर कुछ शब्द हटाकर खाली जगह भरवाने वाली परीक्षा
terms.net: An integrative test in which every nth word of a passage is deleted for the learner to restore; devised by Wilson L. Taylor (1953).

mcqs.q: Who edited Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (1916) from his students' notes?
mcqs.exp: Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye compiled the Cours posthumously.

mcqs.q: Saussure's distinction between language as a system and individual speech is:
mcqs.exp: Langue is the system; parole is the individual utterance.

mcqs.q: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' was used by Chomsky to show that:
options: A sentence can be grammatical but meaningless
mcqs.exp: Chomsky (1957) separated grammaticality from meaningfulness.

mcqs.q: Match the works with the authors: (a) Syntactic Structures (b) How to Do Things with Words (c) Language as Social Semiotic (d) Logic and Conversation | (i) Grice (ii) Halliday (iii) Austin (iv) Chomsky
mcqs.exp: Chomsky 1957; Austin 1962; Halliday 1978; Grice 1975.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of Grice's conversational maxims?
mcqs.exp: Grice's maxims are Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner; politeness is Leech's principle.

mcqs.q: In Austin's theory, the effect of an utterance on the listener is the:
mcqs.exp: Perlocution refers to consequential effects like persuading or frightening.

mcqs.q: Searle's taxonomy of illocutionary acts includes all EXCEPT:
mcqs.exp: Behabitives belong to Austin's classification, not Searle's.

mcqs.q: Halliday's three metafunctions of language are:
mcqs.exp: Field, tenor, mode are register variables; the metafunctions are ideational, interpersonal, textual.

mcqs.q: The term 'phatic communion' was coined by:
mcqs.exp: Malinowski used it in 1923 in a supplement to Ogden and Richards' The Meaning of Meaning.

mcqs.q: Arrange in chronological order: (i) Grimm's Law (ii) Caxton's press (iii) Johnson's Dictionary (iv) Norman Conquest
The term 'Great Vowel Shift' was coined by:
mcqs.exp: Jespersen named the shift of Middle English long vowels.

mcqs.q: The words 'they, them, their' entered English from:
mcqs.exp: These pronouns came from Scandinavian (Old Norse) influence.

mcqs.q: 'Smog' and 'brunch' are examples of:
mcqs.exp: Blends combine parts of two words (smoke + fog).

mcqs.q: 'Edit' derived from 'editor' is an example of:
mcqs.exp: Removing a supposed suffix from an existing word is back-formation.

mcqs.q: Aspirated [ph] in 'pin' and unaspirated [p] in 'spin' are:
mcqs.exp: They are predictable variants of one phoneme in complementary distribution.

mcqs.q: How many phonemes does RP English have?
mcqs.exp: 24 consonants and 20 vowels = 44.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a voiced bilabial plosive?
mcqs.exp: /b/ is voiced, bilabial and plosive; /m/ is a nasal.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): English is a stress-timed language. Reason (R): In English, stressed syllables tend to occur at roughly regular intervals.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true
mcqs.exp: Stress-timing is defined by regular intervals between stressed syllables.

mcqs.q: Leech's 'seven types of meaning' appear in his book:
options: A Linguistic Guide to English Poetry
mcqs.exp: Leech, Semantics (1974) lists conceptual, connotative, social, affective, reflected, collocative and thematic meaning.

mcqs.q: 'Buy/sell' and 'husband/wife' are examples of:
mcqs.exp: Converse (relational) antonyms describe one relation from opposite viewpoints.

mcqs.q: The concept of 'diglossia' was introduced by:
mcqs.exp: Ferguson's 'Diglossia' (1959) described High and Low varieties.

mcqs.q: Basil Bernstein distinguished between:
mcqs.exp: Bernstein linked social class to elaborated and restricted codes.

mcqs.q: In Kachru's model, India belongs to the:
mcqs.exp: Countries where English is a second, institutionalised language form the Outer Circle.

mcqs.q: Which method is based on behaviourist psychology and structural linguistics?
mcqs.exp: ALM uses habit formation through drills, from Skinner and structuralism.

mcqs.q: Match method and founder: (a) Silent Way (b) Suggestopedia (c) TPR (d) Community Language Learning | (i) Asher (ii) Curran (iii) Gattegno (iv) Lozanov
mcqs.exp: Gattegno, Lozanov, Asher and Curran respectively.

mcqs.q: The Bangalore Project associated with Task-Based Language Teaching was led by:
mcqs.exp: N. S. Prabhu ran the Communicational Teaching Project (1979-84).

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of Krashen's five hypotheses?
mcqs.exp: The Output Hypothesis was proposed by Merrill Swain (1985).

mcqs.q: The term 'interlanguage' was coined by:
mcqs.exp: Selinker introduced 'interlanguage' in 1972.

mcqs.q: The effect of a test on teaching and learning is called:
mcqs.exp: Washback (backwash) can be positive or negative.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Neither the teacher nor the students was present.
Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
Neither the teacher or the students were present.
Neither the teacher nor the students is present.
mcqs.exp: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'students'.
